prompt:
Support is triaging a wave of "blank invoice PDF" reports after last week's release. At first glance it looks like the PDF service is broadly broken, which would make it a global outage needing a single fix. But the pattern is oddly specific. The defect IS occurring for: users of the v4.2 desktop app whose account language is set to a right-to-left locale (Arabic or Hebrew) AND who generate invoices using the newer "compact" template. The defect IS NOT occurring for: web and mobile users at all; desktop users on left-to-right locales even with the compact template; RTL-locale users who use the classic template; or anyone on desktop v4.1. Staging, seeded with LTR test accounts only, shows nothing. The rendered PDFs are the correct size and page count but visually empty; server logs show a `200` from the render worker with no error.

The on-call lead says: "The PDF renderer is down, this is a global rendering outage — page the vendor and roll everything back." But the failure clearly discriminates along a three-way intersection (desktop v4.2 × RTL locale × compact template) rather than hitting everyone, and no single suspected cause has been confirmed — it could be a font/shaping issue, a template bug, a client-version regression, or some interaction. Decide whether structured IS/IS-NOT boundary analysis — mapping exactly what is and is not affected to localize the distinguishing dimension — is warranted here, or whether the failure is genuinely global or the cause already known.
decision_instruction: Answer YES if Kepner-Tregoe IS/IS-NOT boundary analysis is warranted because the defect is selective and the cause is unclear. Answer NO if the failure is global or the cause is already known.

prompt:
A finance customer reports the wrong currency symbol on invoices: amounts that should read `€1.234,56` are rendering as `$1,234.56` (dollar sign, US grouping) for some customers. It is not everyone, and nothing obvious changed in the invoice service this week. Investigation so far shows the defect IS present for: customer accounts created before March 2021 that are on the legacy "Standard-2019" billing plan AND have a billing address in a Eurozone country. The defect IS NOT present for: any account created after March 2021; accounts on newer plan types regardless of age; pre-2021 accounts with non-Eurozone addresses; or internal test tenants (all of which were created recently). The amounts themselves are numerically correct — only the currency symbol and digit grouping are wrong. There was no billing deploy in the relevant window, though a shared "locale/formatting" library used by several services was bumped a minor version nine days ago.

A manager insists: "Currency formatting is obviously a global i18n bug in the formatting library — just pin the library back everywhere and move on." But the failure is sharply selective across an intersection of account age, plan type, and geography, and the true cause (stale locale mapping on legacy plans? a data backfill gap? the library bump interacting with old plan records?) has not actually been confirmed. Decide whether Kepner-Tregoe IS/IS-NOT boundary analysis is warranted to pin down the distinguishing factor, or whether this is a global failure with an already-known cause.
decision_instruction: Answer YES if Kepner-Tregoe IS/IS-NOT boundary analysis is warranted because the defect is selective and the cause is unclear. Answer NO if the failure is global or the cause is already known.

prompt:
Checkout is failing for Japanese-yen (JPY) transactions with a processor error `amount_exceeds_maximum`, while USD, EUR, and GBP transactions succeed. On the surface this looks like a classic selective defect — failing for exactly one currency and one region — the kind of thing you'd normally map with an IS/IS-NOT grid. But the payments team has already root-caused it. A refactor merged four days ago introduced a single normalization step that multiplies every transaction amount by 100 before sending it to the processor, on the assumption that all currencies use two minor units (cents). JPY is a zero-decimal currency: an amount is already expressed in whole yen, so the ×100 step inflates every JPY charge 100-fold, pushing typical order totals past the processor's per-transaction maximum and triggering the error. USD/EUR/GBP are two-decimal, so the ×100 step is exactly what those currencies require and they process normally. The offending line is identified, a unit test reproduces it for JPY, and the fix (skip the multiplier for zero-decimal currencies per ISO 4217) is written and in review.

A teammate says: "It only fails for one currency in one country — that's textbook selective, we should run a full IS/IS-NOT boundary analysis before we commit a fix." Given that the exact mechanism, the offending code, and the currency-class distinction are already understood and reproduced, decide whether IS/IS-NOT boundary analysis is warranted, or whether the cause is already known and the selectivity is fully explained.
decision_instruction: Answer YES if Kepner-Tregoe IS/IS-NOT boundary analysis is warranted because the defect is selective and the cause is unclear. Answer NO if the failure is global or the cause is already known.
